title: Revisiting the Aerts-Broekaert-Smets quantum model of the liar paradox
summary: The quantum model of the two-sentence liar paradox proposed by Aerts, Broekaert, and Smets is an early example of the use of quantum formalism to describe cognitive dynamics. Our reconstruction is primarily pedagogical in intent, but it also leads to a number of clarifications, and to some new observations, concerning the structure of the model. Rewriting the model in Dirac notation, we make explicit the distinction between truth values originating from a decision and from semantic inference, and show that the associated enlargement of the one-sentence state space corresponds to a factorization with respect to which the non-paradoxical configurations are separable while the genuine liar state is entangled. We also derive the Hamiltonian generating the four-state cyclic evolution, express it in compact operator form, and give the resulting transition probabilities in closed form. We emphasize that the liar cycle admits a unitarily equivalent representation in the four-dimensional truth-only space, where the unmeasured liar state is separable, so the dimensional enlargement is not required by the unitary part of the dynamics; it is required, however, by the measurement structure. The enlargement is also required by the dynamics as soon as revision processes are admitted, in which states with identical truth content but different origins have different successors, the origin degree of freedom then acting as a minimal form of cognitive memory. We conclude by discussing the possible relationship between the model and more general deliberative processes.

AI.tldr: This paper reconstructs the two-sentence liar paradox quantum model of Aerts, Broekaert, and Smets in Dirac notation, clarifying its structure and offering new observations on entanglement, Hamiltonian dynamics, and the role of state-space enlargement.
AI.motivation: The original quantum model of the two-sentence liar paradox is an early example of quantum formalism applied to cognitive dynamics, but its structure remains opaque in places. The authors aim to clarify the model, distinguish truth values from decision versus semantic inference, and understand why the state-space enlargement is needed.
AI.method: The model is rewritten in Dirac notation. The authors distinguish truth values arising from decision versus semantic inference, analyze the associated factorization of the one-sentence state space, derive the Hamiltonian generating the four-state cyclic evolution, express it in compact operator form, and compute transition probabilities in closed form. They also examine a unitarily equivalent representation in the four-dimensional truth-only space and consider the effect of admitting revision processes.
AI.result: The enlargement of the state space corresponds to a factorization where non-paradoxical configurations are separable but the genuine liar state is entangled. The four-state cyclic evolution has a Hamiltonian expressible in compact operator form with closed-form transition probabilities. The liar cycle has a unitarily equivalent representation in the four-dimensional truth-only space where the unmeasured liar state is separable, so the enlargement is not required by the unitary dynamics alone—it is required by the measurement structure, and also by the dynamics once revision processes are allowed.
AI.conclusion: The dimensional enlargement is not demanded by the unitary part of the dynamics but is required by the measurement structure and by revision processes, where states with identical truth content but different origins have different successors, making the origin degree of freedom a minimal form of cognitive memory. The authors discuss possible links between the model and more general deliberative processes.

title: Persistence of n-Species Lotka-Volterra Models with Periodic Pulses
summary: Periodic impulsive interventions arise naturally in the management of biological populations, including chemotherapy, pesticide application, and infectious-disease treatment. We develop general conditions for permanence in n-species population models subject to periodic multiplicative pulse disturbances. Our main result provides a sufficient condition for permanence in terms of weighted long-term growth rates on a Morse decomposition of the extinction set, explicitly separating the contributions of continuous population dynamics from those of the periodic pulse. To establish this result, we transform the impulsive system into an associated autonomous continuous-time dynamical system and use this correspondence to extend classical permanence theory to periodically pulsed models. We further show that the same conditions imply robust permanence under sufficiently small perturbations to the continuous dynamics, pulse period, and pulse effects. We illustrate the framework with two Lotka-Volterra models motivated by biological control: competition between chemotherapy-sensitive and chemotherapy-resistant cancer cells, and integrated control of an agricultural pest using pesticides and parasitoids. These examples demonstrate how intervention frequency and intensity interact with underlying ecological interactions to determine whether populations coexist or are excluded. Our results provide a general framework for analyzing persistence in ecological systems subject to repeated discrete disturbances.

AI.tldr: This paper derives general sufficient conditions for permanence (and robust permanence) in n-species population models under periodic multiplicative pulse disturbances, and illustrates them with two Lotka-Volterra biological control examples.
AI.motivation: Periodic impulsive interventions (chemotherapy, pesticide application, infectious-disease treatment) are common in population management, but classical permanence theory does not directly handle models with discrete periodic pulses, so a general framework is needed.
AI.method: The impulsive system is transformed into an associated autonomous continuous-time dynamical system, allowing classical permanence theory (via Morse decomposition of the extinction set and weighted long-term growth rates) to be extended; conditions separate the roles of continuous dynamics and periodic pulses, and robustness under small perturbations is also analyzed.
AI.result: A sufficient condition for permanence is given in terms of weighted long-term growth rates on the extinction set's Morse decomposition; the same conditions yield robust permanence under small perturbations to dynamics, pulse period, and pulse effects. Two Lotka-Volterra examples (chemo-sensitive vs. resistant cancer cells; pesticide-plus-parasitoid pest control) show how intervention frequency and intensity interact with ecological interactions to determine coexistence vs. exclusion.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a general framework for analyzing persistence in ecological systems subject to repeated discrete disturbances.

title: Population Ecology of Tunes
summary: How cultural repertoires maintain diversity under selection is a fundamental question in cultural evolution. We address this using thirteen years of weekly popularity data for approximately 20,000 Irish traditional tunes, fitting ecological birth-process models under neutral, frequency-dependent, and per-tune selection hypotheses. We find strong evidence that tunes differ in intrinsic fitness - some are systematically more likely to be learned than others. We find that 29% of the variance in fitness can be explained by a mixture of social and melodic features. Some tunes appear to be carried along via linkage due to the tradition of playing tunes in sets, analogous to selective sweeps in genetics. By measuring changes in fitness over time and comparing this with recordings we precisely identify the mechanism by which a long-dormant tune can become fit through a popular recording. Despite the directional selection, repertoire diversity increases, driven by the continual arrival of new compositions. These results demonstrate that selection and diversity can coexist in a cultural ecosystem, and establish Irish traditional music as a quantitatively tractable system for studying the evolution of cultural variants and understanding what makes a tune stand out.

AI.tldr: Using 13 years of weekly popularity data for ~20,000 Irish traditional tunes, the authors fit ecological birth-process models to show that tunes differ in intrinsic fitness, yet repertoire diversity still increases due to continual arrival of new compositions.
AI.motivation: How cultural repertoires maintain diversity under selection is a fundamental question in cultural evolution. Irish traditional music offers a large, well-documented dataset to test whether selection and diversity can coexist.
AI.method: Fit ecological birth-process models under neutral, frequency-dependent, and per-tune selection hypotheses to weekly popularity data for ~20,000 Irish traditional tunes over thirteen years. Analyze fitness variance explained by social and melodic features, linkage via tune sets, and fitness changes over time compared with recordings.
AI.result: Strong evidence that tunes differ in intrinsic fitness. 29% of fitness variance is explained by a mixture of social and melodic features. Some tunes are carried along via linkage from the tradition of playing tunes in sets (analogous to selective sweeps). The mechanism by which a long-dormant tune becomes fit through a popular recording is precisely identified. Repertoire diversity nevertheless increases due to continual arrival of new compositions.
AI.conclusion: Selection and diversity can coexist in a cultural ecosystem. Irish traditional music is established as a quantitatively tractable system for studying cultural variant evolution and understanding what makes a tune stand out.

title: Multi-Task Bacterial Colony Detection and Classification Using YOLOv8 with Edge Optimization for Resource-Constrained Deployment
summary: Manual counting and classification of bacterial colonies are critical yet labor-intensive tasks in microbiology, prone to human error particularly on densely populated plates. This work proposes a multi-task deep learning framework trained on the Annotated Germs for Automated Recognition (AGAR) dataset (18,000 images; 9,202 training / 3,067 testing) to automate Colony Forming Unit (CFU) enumeration and species classification. A custom multi-task CNN employing global regression served as the baseline, but demonstrated limited performance in clustered colony environments due to the absence of spatial localization. To address this, a YOLOv8 object detection architecture was adopted with high-resolution 1024x1024 inputs, enabling instance-level colony detection and label assignment. The model achieved a classification accuracy of 98.13% and a counting accuracy of 98.27% (within a 10-colony margin), demonstrating strong predictive capability. To bridge the gap between model performance and practical deployability, the trained model was optimized through unstructured and structured pruning, ONNX conversion, and reduced-precision inference (FP32, FP16, INT8). On a Raspberry Pi 4B, ONNX FP32 and FP16 variants offered the best balance between inference speed (~6.4s) and accuracy (MAE ~2.20). Unstructured pruning preserved predictive accuracy (MAE ~2.01) without runtime gains, while structured pruning resulted in significant accuracy degradation (MAE ~6.3), revealing the sensitivity of instance-level colony detection to architectural compression. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting optimization strategies in resource-constrained laboratory deployments.

AI.tldr: A YOLOv8-based multi-task framework automates bacterial colony counting and species classification on the AGAR dataset, achieving ~98% accuracy, then is optimized via pruning and quantized ONNX inference for Raspberry Pi deployment.
AI.motivation: Manual counting and classification of bacterial colonies are labor-intensive and error-prone, especially on densely populated plates, motivating automated deep learning solutions that can run in resource-constrained laboratory settings.
AI.method: Trained on the AGAR dataset (18,000 images; 9,202 train / 3,067 test). A custom multi-task CNN with global regression served as baseline but failed in clustered colonies due to lack of spatial localization. Replaced with YOLOv8 object detection at 1024x1024 resolution for instance-level detection and label assignment. Deployment optimization via unstructured and structured pruning, ONNX conversion, and reduced-precision inference (FP32, FP16, INT8).
AI.result: Classification accuracy 98.13%, counting accuracy 98.27% (within 10-colony margin). On Raspberry Pi 4B, ONNX FP32/FP16 gave best trade-off (~6.4s inference, MAE ~2.20). Unstructured pruning preserved accuracy (MAE ~2.01) with no runtime gains; structured pruning degraded accuracy significantly (MAE ~6.3).
AI.conclusion: YOLOv8-based instance-level detection is highly effective for colony counting and classification, but instance-level detection is sensitive to architectural compression. ONNX FP32/FP16 quantization offers the best practical balance for edge deployment, providing guidance for optimization strategy selection in resource-constrained labs.

title: Thermodynamic and Statistical Signatures of Modality Changes in Concentration Distributions Driven by Stochastic Switching Between Two Activity States
summary: Stochastic switching between gene expression states, coupled with production and degradation dynamics, governs the accumulation of mRNA and proteins in cells. The concentrations of these accumulated entities dictate the phenotypic distribution of genetically identical cells. The underlying accumulation dynamics are well-captured by a two-state promoter switching model, with statistical and thermodynamic properties quantified via the Fano factor and entropy production rates. However, how these measures correlate with concentration distributions and their shifts under varying kinetic parameters remains largely unexplored. To this end, we use chemical master equations to study a generalized model of mRNA accumulation dynamics in the presence of stochastic switching between two activity states and state-dependent production and degradation rates. We derive exact expressions for the steady-state probability distribution and analytically compute the mean concentration, Fano factor, and entropy production rate (EPR). Simplifying these expressions, we identify contributions arising from stochastic switching rates and relaxation dynamics toward equilibrium in each activity state. Next, using our theoretical results, we characterize the variation in the Fano factor and EPR as a function of mean expression during modality changes of the distributions mediated by the variation of switching rates. We also identify the conditions in kinetic parameters that achieve the highest Fano factor and entropy production rates. Our findings establish a generalized framework for examining stochastic accumulation dynamics, clarifying how kinetic parameters dictate molecular distributions, noise, and dissipation. These insights extend readily to broader contexts coupling stochastic switching with accumulation, including protein burst dynamics, phenotype-switching-mediated drug intake, and queuing theory.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a generalized two-state promoter switching model for mRNA accumulation, deriving exact steady-state distributions and analytically computing mean concentration, Fano factor, and entropy production rate (EPR) to reveal how kinetic parameters shape molecular distributions, noise, and dissipation.
AI.motivation: Stochastic switching between gene expression states combined with production/degradation dynamics governs mRNA/protein accumulation and phenotype distributions. While the two-state promoter switching model is well-established and quantified via Fano factor and EPR, how these measures correlate with concentration distributions and shift under varying kinetic parameters remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors use chemical master equations to study a generalized mRNA accumulation model with stochastic switching between two activity states and state-dependent production and degradation rates. They derive exact steady-state probability distributions and analytically compute mean concentration, Fano factor, and EPR, then simplify expressions to isolate contributions from switching rates and relaxation dynamics.
AI.result: They characterize how Fano factor and EPR vary with mean expression across modality changes driven by switching rates, and identify kinetic parameter conditions that maximize Fano factor and EPR.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a generalized framework for stochastic accumulation dynamics, clarifying how kinetic parameters dictate molecular distributions, noise, and dissipation. It extends to protein burst dynamics, phenotype-switching-mediated drug intake, and queuing theory.

title: ADMET-EvO: a self-evolving scientific agent for sustained research across heterogeneous tasks
summary: Scientific agents can move beyond automated model building by using accumulated evidence to revise both their questions and experimental strategies. The challenge is sustaining this adaptation across heterogeneous tasks without overfitting decisions to internal validation. Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) prediction provides a demanding setting across diverse assays, datasets and chemical domains. We therefore developed ADMET-EvO, an evidence-gated agent that formalizes endpoints, generates falsifiable hypotheses and tests interventions across data, feature and model axes. It carries supported, rejected and inconclusive outcomes forward to guide each new cycle. Across the 22-task Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) ADMET benchmark, ADMET-EvO achieved the highest task-normalized score of 96.77. Evidence-guided selection reduced cumulative fitting time by 72.2% within a predefined non-inferiority margin. It also formalized 43 toxicity-related tasks and constructed endpoint-specific predictors. Together, these results show how ADMET-EvO can accumulate evidence, revise its strategy and expand its research scope over time.

AI.tldr: ADMET-EvO is an evidence-gated scientific agent that formalizes endpoints, generates falsifiable hypotheses, and tests interventions across data/feature/model axes, achieving the best task-normalized score (96.77) on the 22-task TDC ADMET benchmark.
AI.motivation: Scientific agents should go beyond automated model building by using accumulated evidence to revise their questions and experimental strategies, but sustaining this adaptation across heterogeneous tasks without overfitting to internal validation is challenging. ADMET prediction offers a demanding testbed across diverse assays, datasets, and chemical domains.
AI.method: ADMET-EvO formalizes endpoints, generates falsifiable hypotheses, and tests interventions along data, feature, and model axes. It carries supported, rejected, and inconclusive outcomes forward to guide each new cycle (evidence-gated loop).
AI.result: On the 22-task TDC ADMET benchmark, it achieved the highest task-normalized score of 96.77. Evidence-guided selection cut cumulative fitting time by 72.2% within a predefined non-inferiority margin. It also formalized 43 toxicity-related tasks and built endpoint-specific predictors.
AI.conclusion: ADMET-EvO can accumulate evidence, revise its strategy, and expand its research scope over time, demonstrating effective self-adapting scientific agents.

title: Are You Learning Biological Signal or Shortcuts? Auditing and Mitigating Bias in Protein-Protein Interaction Datasets
summary: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases do not faithfully reflect biological realities. Instead, they are influenced by study and technical biases that distort certain protein and interaction attributes. Machine learning models can exploit these as learning shortcuts if the negative dataset is not constructed with care. So far, the shortcuts introduced during PPI dataset construction have only been examined in isolation. Here, we systematically characterize both reported and, to our knowledge, previously unreported biases in PPI datasets that lead machine learning models to learn shortcuts instead of biological signal. We analyze HIPPIE, IntAct, and STRING, dedicated PPI databases, as well as two datasets derived from 3D-structural information in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). We show that random data splitting introduces strong topological shortcuts. When train-test protein overlap is removed, the resulting datasets still retain usable shortcuts stemming from self-interactions, taxonomic identity, and functional relatedness, whose prevalence interestingly depends on the data source. We further show that sampling negatives from a set of high-confidence non-interactors, an intuitively appealing choice, can amplify the shortcut stemming from functional relatedness. To detect and mitigate these biases, we provide an open Nextflow pipeline that combines similarity-aware, data-loss-minimizing dataset splitting with bias-minimizing negative sampling, both formulated as integer linear programs. Its key concept of quantifying biases to minimize them through optimization-based negative sampling can, in principle, be extended to any machine learning problem where the pool of negative candidates is much larger than the positives and is thus of interest also beyond PPI prediction.

AI.tldr: PPI datasets contain study and technical biases that machine learning models exploit as shortcuts. This work systematically characterizes known and previously unreported biases across HIPPIE, IntAct, STRING, and two PDB-derived datasets, and provides an open Nextflow pipeline using integer linear programs for similarity-aware splitting and bias-minimizing negative sampling.
AI.motivation: PPI databases do not faithfully reflect biological reality; they are distorted by study and technical biases. Machine learning models can exploit these biases as shortcuts if negative datasets are not carefully constructed. Prior work examined these shortcuts only in isolation.
AI.method: Systematically characterize reported and previously unreported biases in PPI datasets from HIPPIE, IntAct, STRING, and two PDB 3D-structure-derived datasets. Develop an open Nextflow pipeline combining similarity-aware, data-loss-minimizing dataset splitting and bias-minimizing negative sampling, both formulated as integer linear programs.
AI.result: Random data splitting introduces strong topological shortcuts. After removing train-test protein overlap, datasets still retain usable shortcuts from self-interactions, taxonomic identity, and functional relatedness, whose prevalence depends on the data source. Sampling negatives from high-confidence non-interactors can amplify the functional-relatedness shortcut.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline detects and mitigates these biases. The key concept of quantifying biases to minimize them through optimization-based negative sampling can extend to any machine learning problem where negative candidates greatly outnumber positives, beyond PPI prediction.

title: On the spectral radius properties of a key matrix in periodic impulse control
summary: In this work, we consider the periodic impulse control of a system modeled as a set of linear differential equations. We define a matrix that governs the qualitative behavior of the controlled system. This matrix depends on the period and effects of the control interventions. We investigate properties of the spectral radius of this matrix and in particular, how it depends on the period of the interventions. Our main result is on the convexity of the spectral radius with respect to this period. We discuss implications of this convexity on establishing an optimal and maximum period for effective control. Finally, we provide an example motivated from a real-life scenario.

AI.tldr: This paper studies periodic impulse control of linear differential equation systems, analyzing a governing matrix whose spectral radius depends on the intervention period, and proves its convexity with respect to that period.
AI.motivation: Periodic impulse control governs the qualitative behavior of linear systems, and understanding how the intervention period affects stability is key to designing effective control strategies.
AI.method: The authors define a matrix characterizing the controlled system's behavior (dependent on period and control effects), then investigate properties of its spectral radius, proving convexity with respect to the period.
AI.result: The main result establishes convexity of the spectral radius as a function of the intervention period.
AI.conclusion: This convexity enables determination of an optimal and maximum period for effective control, illustrated with a real-life example.

title: Adaptive Entangled Game Modules in Artificial General Intelligence
summary: We introduce a probability-wave framework for modeling the collective behavior of interacting adaptive agents, deriving testable eigenmodes through a generalized behavioral intelligence (GBI) nonlocal probability-wave equation. This framework captures a broad range of human intelligence behaviors with analytical mechanisms and offers an indirect method to examine the Liu-Chen-Ao (LCA) hypothesis of nonlocal entangled nerve fibers in the brain through collective trader behaviors. Our empirical analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data demonstrates that adaptive entangled game modes explain 82-94% (89% overall) of observed decision patterns, a sharp contrast to the predictions of neoclassical finance based on independent rational agents. Moreover, 2-12% of behaviors show adaption to intraday news, events, and environments, characterized by dual equilibrium states and abrupt reference point shifts, while purely independent modes occur in less than 5% of cases. These findings empirically support the LCA hypothesis, as observable trading behaviors reflect underlying brain mechanisms and internal intelligence decision-making in behavioral psychology. Our results highlight the necessity of incorporating adaptive entangled game modules into artificial general intelligence (AGI) architectures, addressing the limitations of conventional artificial neural network (ANN)-based AI, which relies on trillions of opaque parameters. By integrating ANN-based AI with probability-wave-based entangled-brain simulations, machine learning can enrich AGI foundation models (FMs) and facilitate the development of human-like processing units (HPUs) that leverage brain-inspired mechanisms. Such HPUs may ultimately create more compact, efficient, and robust AGI systems, particularly for embodied intelligence and robotics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a probability-wave framework with a generalized behavioral intelligence (GBI) nonlocal probability-wave equation to model collective behavior of adaptive agents, and uses Chinese stock market data to test the Liu-Chen-Ao hypothesis on nonlocal entangled nerve fibers.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to offer an indirect empirical method to examine the LCA hypothesis of nonlocal entangled nerve fibers, and to address limitations of conventional ANN-based AI that relies on trillions of opaque parameters.
AI.method: They derive testable eigenmodes via the GBI nonlocal probability-wave equation and apply the framework to empirical analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data, comparing adaptive entangled game modes against neoclassical independent-rational-agent predictions.
AI.result: Adaptive entangled game modes explain 82-94% (89% overall) of decision patterns; 2-12% of behaviors adapt to intraday news/events/environments with dual equilibrium states and abrupt reference point shifts; purely independent modes occur in under 5% of cases.
AI.conclusion: Findings support the LCA hypothesis and suggest integrating adaptive entangled game modules into AGI architectures, combining ANN-based AI with probability-wave entangled-brain simulations to enable compact, efficient human-like processing units (HPUs) for embodied intelligence and robotics.

title: Stable Coexistence in Ecologies and Games
summary: We study feasible stable equilibria of Lotka-Volterra systems and their higher-order extensions. We complete the classification of impossible ecological interaction networks with at most four species and extend several of these impossibility results to families with arbitrarily many species. We then show that these sign-pattern obstructions are specific to the pairwise Lotka-Volterra model: arbitrary prescribed growth rates and pairwise coefficients can be supplemented by higher-order interactions so as to admit a feasible asymptotically stable equilibrium. Through the correspondence with replicator dynamics, we interpret feasible equilibria of higher-order Lotka-Volterra systems as totally mixed symmetric Nash equilibria of symmetric multiplayer games, derive bounds on their number, and study their robustness under perturbations of the payoff tensors. We conclude by showing that every impossible ecology determines a nonempty open class of symmetric two-player games with no totally mixed evolutionarily stable strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies feasible stable equilibria in Lotka-Volterra systems and shows higher-order interactions can overcome pairwise impossibility results, with game-theoretic interpretations.
AI.motivation: Understanding which ecological interaction networks can sustain stable coexistence is a fundamental question. Prior work identified impossible sign patterns for pairwise Lotka-Volterra systems, but the scope of these obstructions and whether they persist under higher-order interactions remained unclear.
AI.method: The authors classify impossible ecological interaction networks with at most four species, extend impossibility results to arbitrary numbers of species, add higher-order interaction terms to arbitrary prescribed pairwise systems, and use the correspondence between Lotka-Volterra systems and replicator dynamics to reinterpret equilibria as Nash equilibria of symmetric multiplayer games.
AI.result: They complete the classification of impossible networks for up to four species, extend several impossibility results to larger families, show that arbitrary pairwise coefficients can be stabilized via higher-order interactions, derive bounds on the number of totally mixed symmetric Nash equilibria, study robustness under payoff perturbations, and show every impossible ecology yields an open class of symmetric two-player games with no totally mixed ESS.
AI.conclusion: Sign-pattern obstructions are specific to pairwise Lotka-Volterra models and disappear with higher-order interactions, linking ecological impossibility to the absence of totally mixed evolutionarily stable strategies in games.

title: A thermodynamically consistent framework for finite growth of multi-constituent mixtures with application to tumor growth
summary: Biological tissues grow by continuously producing, transporting, and reorganizing multiple interacting constituents. These processes are intrinsically coupled to finite deformation and residual stress. Existing models typically capture either finite growth kinematics or multi-constituent transport, but rarely both within a thermodynamically consistent setting. In particular, existing approaches do not consistently link the volume created by finite growth to the mass produced for each individual constituent. In this work, we develop a general continuum framework that unifies finite growth kinematics and multiphase mixture theory for fully saturated multi-constituent mixtures containing an arbitrary number of dilute dissolved solutes. Formulated in a solid-skeleton-based description, the framework rests on constituent-wise balance laws and a free-energy dissipation principle, from which thermodynamically admissible constitutive closures are derived for all mass-exchange, transport, reaction, and growth processes. The central novelty of the framework is a coupling between growth-induced volume creation and constituent mass production, expressed through volume accumulation fractions that distribute the newly created volume among the constituents while preserving saturation. We cast the resulting model in a total Lagrangian mixed weak form and specialize the general theory to a four-constituent, two-solute model of avascular tumor growth that couples nutrient transport, waste production, phenotype transitions between proliferative, hypoxic, and necrotic cells, volume growth, elastic deformation, and growth-induced residual stress. The model is implemented within a finite element setting and its capabilities are demonstrated on representative benchmark problems.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a thermodynamically consistent continuum framework unifying finite growth kinematics with multiphase mixture theory for saturated multi-constituent mixtures, introducing volume accumulation fractions to couple growth-induced volume creation with constituent mass production.
AI.motivation: Existing models capture either finite growth kinematics or multi-constituent transport, but rarely both in a thermodynamically consistent manner. Notably, they fail to consistently link the volume created by finite growth to the mass produced for each individual constituent.
AI.method: A general continuum framework formulated in a solid-skeleton-based description, built on constituent-wise balance laws and a free-energy dissipation principle to derive thermodynamically admissible constitutive closures for mass-exchange, transport, reaction, and growth. The key novelty is volume accumulation fractions distributing newly created volume among constituents while preserving saturation. The model is cast in a total Lagrangian mixed weak form and specialized to a four-constituent, two-solute avascular tumor growth model.
AI.result: The specialized model couples nutrient transport, waste production, phenotype transitions (proliferative, hypoxic, necrotic), volume growth, elastic deformation, and growth-induced residual stress. It is implemented in a finite element setting and demonstrated on benchmark problems.
AI.conclusion: The framework unifies finite growth kinematics and multiphase mixture theory with thermodynamic consistency, offering a general tool for modeling multi-constituent biological tissue growth and demonstrated via tumor growth simulations.

title: XAI-Refine: An Automated Explanation-Knowledge Loop for Brain-Age Prediction
summary: Brain-age prediction models are commonly evaluated by predictive accuracy, yet accurate predictions alone do not establish that a model relies on reproducible or neurobiologically supported mechanisms. Post-hoc explanation methods can expose these mechanisms, but existing workflows typically stop at diagnosis or require correction targets to be specified before model analysis. We propose XAI-Refine, an automated explanation-knowledge loop for brain-age prediction from resting-state functional connectivity. At each iteration, XAI-Refine consolidates complementary post-hoc analyses across repeated training runs into reliable, structured model explanations. It converts each reliable explanation into a neutral neurobiological question, retrieves and verifies relevant literature, and compiles the verified evidence into an admissible set in the same typed explanation space. The target for refinement is defined as the minimal projection of the current model explanation onto the admissible set induced by applicable verified knowledge. This revised explanation is then translated into a differentiable constraint while preserving the originating model variable, measurement operator, and applicable scope. Candidate updates are promoted only when multi-seed validation confirms target-directed explanatory movement, predictive performance remains within a prespecified guardrail, and non-target explanatory drift remains bounded. Experiments on functional-connectivity-based brain-age prediction evaluate predictive performance, explanation reliability, literature alignment, and target-specific model revision, illustrating a structured route from post-hoc analysis to evidence-guided model refinement.

AI.tldr: XAI-Refine is an automated explanation-knowledge loop that turns reliable post-hoc explanations of brain-age prediction models into neurobiological questions, verifies them against literature, and translates the resulting admissible knowledge into differentiable constraints to guide model refinement.
AI.motivation: Predictive accuracy alone does not guarantee that brain-age models rely on reproducible or neurobiologically supported mechanisms. Existing post-hoc explanation workflows either stop at diagnosis or require correction targets to be specified before model analysis, preventing systematic evidence-guided refinement.
AI.method: At each iteration, XAI-Refine consolidates complementary post-hoc analyses across repeated training runs into structured, reliable explanations. Each reliable explanation is converted into a neutral neurobiological question; relevant literature is retrieved and verified; verified evidence is compiled into an admissible set in the same typed explanation space. The refinement target is the minimal projection of the current model explanation onto this admissible set, translated into a differentiable constraint while preserving model variable, measurement operator, and scope. Updates are promoted only if multi-seed validation confirms target-directed movement, predictive performance stays within a guardrail, and non-target explanatory drift is bounded.
AI.result: Experiments on functional-connectivity-based brain-age prediction assess predictive performance, explanation reliability, literature alignment, and target-specific model revision, demonstrating a structured route from post-hoc analysis to evidence-guided model refinement.
AI.conclusion: XAI-Refine provides an automated loop bridging post-hoc explanation and neurobiological literature to refine brain-age prediction models toward evidence-supported mechanisms while safeguarding predictive accuracy and limiting unintended explanatory drift.

title: Emergence of criticality in models of real neurons
summary: Critical systems sit near boundaries between qualitatively distinct behaviors. When inferring models of neural activity, this proximity to criticality is thought to require the precise tuning of parameters. Here, we show that as the number of neurons increases, criticality can emerge naturally without fine-tuning. When computing observable statistics from parameters (the forward problem), some small regions in parameter space map to large regions in statistics space. These special parameters are precisely those near criticality. Thus, when inferring parameters from experimental measurements (the inverse problem), models concentrate near critical points, and this concentration becomes stronger as the system grows. We illustrate this flow toward criticality across many large-scale recordings in the mouse brain. In the Curie-Weiss model of Ising spins, we find that all of the recordings collapse to a first-order phase transition, despite substantial differences in the underlying systems. Together, these results suggest a resolution to the tension between criticality and fine-tuning in models of neural activity.

AI.tldr: As neural population size grows, criticality emerges naturally without fine-tuning because inferring parameters from statistics concentrates models near critical points, illustrated across large-scale mouse brain recordings.
AI.motivation: Critical systems sit near boundaries between qualitatively distinct behaviors, and models of neural activity are thought to require precise parameter tuning to reach criticality, creating tension between criticality and fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors analyze the forward problem (parameters to statistics) showing that small parameter regions near criticality map to large statistics regions, then study the inverse problem (statistics to parameters) and apply this to Curie-Weiss Ising model fits across many large-scale mouse brain recordings.
AI.result: Inference concentrates models near critical points, and this concentration strengthens with system size. All recordings collapse to a first-order phase transition in the Curie-Weiss model despite substantial underlying differences.
AI.conclusion: Criticality can emerge naturally without fine-tuning as neuron number increases, resolving the tension between criticality and fine-tuning in neural activity models.

title: CHIMERA Challenge Task 2 and 3: Response Subtypes Classification and Progression Survival Prediction in Bladder Cancer Patients using Multimodal Datasets
comment: 53 pages, 9 figures, including supplementary material. Catherine Chia and Tongjie Wang contributed equally and share first authorship. Submitted to Medical Image Analysis
summary: High-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (HR-NMIBC) carries substantial risks of recurrence and progression, while current clinical risk stratification remains limited. CHIMERA was established as a multimodal AI challenge to benchmark prediction in HR-NMIBC under standardized evaluation. Task BRS predicts RNA-seq-defined BCG Response Subtypes from histopathology and structured clinicopathological data, whereas Task Progression models time-to-progression using histopathology, structured data, and RNA sequencing. A multimodal dataset of 368 patients was divided into public training and hidden validation and test sets. In total, 159 submissions were made, and 13 top-performing models were selected for benchmarking. The best models achieved a weighted F1 score of 0.73 for Task BRS and a C-index of 0.68 for Task Progression. Post-challenge analyses revealed task-dependent modality contributions, cohort-dependent performance degradation, and sensitivity to missing structured data. In Task BRS, histopathology partly compensated for pathology-derived structured variables, whereas progression models showed greater dependence on complementary inputs. Cross-model error analysis further identified patients that were consistently difficult across different architectures, with T1 substage associated with prediction difficulty. These findings highlight barriers to transportability and the importance of missingness-aware modeling and independent multi-institutional validation. CHIMERA provides a standardized multimodal benchmark for bladder cancer and a framework for studying not only model performance, but also robustness, information sufficiency, and patient-level prediction failure.

AI.tldr: CHIMERA is a multimodal AI challenge benchmarking prediction of BCG response subtypes and progression in high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer using a 368-patient dataset, with best models reaching F1 0.73 (BRS) and C-index 0.68 (Progression).
AI.motivation: HR-NMIBC carries high recurrence and progression risks, but current clinical risk stratification is limited, motivating a standardized multimodal benchmark for robust prediction.
AI.method: A multimodal dataset of 368 patients (public training + hidden validation/test) with histopathology, structured clinicopathological data, and RNA-seq. Task BRS predicts RNA-seq-defined BCG Response Subtypes; Task Progression models time-to-progression. 159 submissions yielded 13 top models for benchmarking.
AI.result: Best models achieved weighted F1 0.73 (BRS) and C-index 0.68 (Progression). Analyses showed task-dependent modality contributions, cohort-dependent performance degradation, and sensitivity to missing structured data; histopathology partly compensated for pathology-derived variables in BRS, while progression relied more on complementary inputs. T1 substage was linked to prediction difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Findings highlight barriers to transportability and the need for missingness-aware modeling and independent multi-institutional validation. CHIMERA provides a standardized multimodal benchmark and framework for studying model robustness, information sufficiency, and patient-level prediction failure.

title: EEGBind: Detecting Source-Level Interictal Epileptiform Discharges via EEG-Centric Multimodal Binding
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (MM '26)
summary: Source-level analysis of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) is relevant to presurgical evaluation and treatment planning because it helps characterize where epileptiform activity is likely to arise. Beyond detecting whether an IED is present, this setting requires assigning IED-positive activity to clinically meaningful brain-region categories. This setting is challenging because source-region evidence in short electroencephalography (EEG) windows can be subtle, partial, and affected by subject variability, class imbalance, and imperfect multimodal context. We present EEGBind, an EEG-centric multimodal binding framework for five-class source-level IED classification. EEGBind treats EEG as the primary modality and binds synchronized video-context features around an EEG-centric representation. Instead of relying on early or overly strong multimodal fusion, which may perturb the source-sensitive EEG representation, EEGBind uses video context as auxiliary evidence for robust classification. A view-consistent repair stage is further used to improve hidden-set robustness while preserving the learned source-class boundary. On the NeuroMM 2026 Grand Challenge Track 3 NMM-Source-IED benchmark, EEGBind achieves 0.8395 on weighted-F1 and outperforms strong competitors. These results support EEG-centric multimodal binding as a practical strategy for source-level IED classification. The open-source code is available at https://github.com/HKUSTGZ-ML4Health-Lab/NeuroMM2026_IED_Detection.

AI.tldr: EEGBind is an EEG-centric multimodal framework that binds video context as auxiliary evidence to classify source-level interictal epileptiform discharges into five brain-region classes, achieving 0.8395 weighted-F1 on the NeuroMM 2026 NMM-Source-IED benchmark.
AI.motivation: Source-level analysis of IEDs aids presurgical evaluation by localizing where epileptiform activity arises, requiring assignment of IED-positive activity to clinically meaningful brain regions rather than mere detection. This is hard because source-region evidence in short EEG windows is subtle, partial, and complicated by subject variability, class imbalance, and imperfect multimodal context.
AI.method: EEGBind is an EEG-centric multimodal binding framework for five-class source-level IED classification. It treats EEG as the primary modality and binds synchronized video-context features around an EEG-centric representation, using video context as auxiliary evidence instead of early or overly strong fusion that could perturb the source-sensitive EEG representation. A view-consistent repair stage improves hidden-set robustness while preserving the learned source-class boundary.
AI.result: On the NeuroMM 2026 Grand Challenge Track 3 NMM-Source-IED benchmark, EEGBind achieves 0.8395 weighted-F1 and outperforms strong competitors.
AI.conclusion: The results support EEG-centric multimodal binding as a practical strategy for source-level IED classification.

title: ProMeta: Few-shot PROTAC-targeted degradation prediction across E3 ligases
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, and 2 tables. Source code and reproducibility resources are available at https://github.com/yeyufeiyyf/prometa and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21371599
summary: Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) have emerged as a transformative therapeutic strategy that selectively degrades historically ''undruggable'' targets via the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Despite growing efforts to develop computational predictors of PROTAC degradation activity, existing supervised approaches remain severely challenged by data scarcity and imbalance across E3 ligases, limiting their ability to generalize beyond well-studied ligase contexts. In practice, labeled data are heavily concentrated on a few ligases (e.g., CRBN and VHL), while the majority of E3 ligases remain underexplored yet are critical for expanding the design space of targeted degraders. Developing methods that enable robust cross-ligase generalization with minimal labeled data is therefore essential for improving the practical utility of computational PROTAC discovery. We reformulate PROTAC degradation activity prediction across E3 ligases as a few-shot meta-learning problem and present ProMeta, a prototype-based graph neural network trained through episodic meta-learning on source-E3 tasks and evaluated on held-out target-E3 tasks through support-conditioned inference. ProMeta performs inference without updating the encoder by dynamically estimating class prototypes from minimal target-ligase support samples. On the CRBN-to-VHL benchmark, ProMeta achieves AUROC values of 0.796 under K=2, Q=3 and 0.883 under K=2, Q=5, improving by 19.9% and 6.8%, respectively, over the corresponding supervised GNN baseline. Reverse VHL-to-CRBN transfer under the same protocol yielded AUROC values of 0.702 (K=2, Q=3) and 0.821 (K=2, Q=5), confirming bidirectional applicability while revealing direction and data-regime dependence. Together, these results support ProMeta as a practical framework for cross-ligase few-shot prediction under the evaluated support/query protocols.

AI.tldr: ProMeta reformulates PROTAC degradation activity prediction as a few-shot meta-learning problem, using a prototype-based GNN to achieve robust cross-E3-ligase generalization with minimal labeled data.
AI.motivation: PROTACs selectively degrade "undruggable" targets, but computational predictors suffer from data scarcity and imbalance across E3 ligases (data concentrated on CRBN/VHL), limiting cross-ligase generalization.
AI.method: ProMeta is a prototype-based graph neural network trained via episodic meta-learning on source-E3 tasks, evaluated on held-out target-E3 tasks through support-conditioned inference, estimating class prototypes dynamically without updating the encoder.
AI.result: CRBN-to-VHL: AUROC 0.796 (K=2,Q=3) and 0.883 (K=2,Q=5), improving 19.9% and 6.8% over supervised GNN baseline. Reverse VHL-to-CRBN: AUROC 0.702 and 0.821, confirming bidirectional applicability with direction/data-regime dependence.
AI.conclusion: ProMeta is a practical framework for cross-ligase few-shot PROTAC degradation prediction under evaluated support/query protocols.

title: A Bio-Plausible Visual Neural Network for Locust-Inspired Collision Perception
summary: Locust visual systems have long served as an important biological paradigm for studying looming perception and collision avoidance. Numerous computational models have successfully reproduced the selective responses of Lobula Giant Movement Detector (LGMD) neurons to approaching objects, thereby emulating the fundamental functionality of the biological system. However, existing models remain limited in biological plausibility and robustness when operating in complex and dynamic visual environments. To address these limitations, we propose a biologically plausible neural network for locust-inspired looming detection. The proposed framework incorporates a spatially isotropic sampling strategy that mimics the ommatidial organization of the locust compound eye, a population-voting mechanism inspired by population coding in biological neural systems, and leaky integrate-and-fire neuronal dynamics to replace conventional sigmoid-based membrane activation. Systematic experiments on synthetic stimuli, laboratory sequences, and real-world driving scenarios demonstrate that the proposed model improves robustness under challenging visual conditions while preserving computational efficiency and enhancing biological fidelity. These results highlight the potential of biologically grounded neural computation for robust and efficient collision perception.

AI.tldr: A biologically plausible neural network for locust-inspired looming detection improves robustness in complex visual environments by mimicking compound eye sampling, population coding, and leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics.
AI.motivation: Locust visual systems are a key paradigm for looming perception. Existing computational models of LGMD neurons are limited in biological plausibility and robustness in complex, dynamic visual environments.
AI.method: Proposes a biologically plausible network incorporating a spatially isotropic sampling strategy mimicking ommatidial organization, a population-voting mechanism inspired by population coding, and leaky integrate-and-fire neuronal dynamics replacing sigmoid-based membrane activation.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic stimuli, laboratory sequences, and real-world driving scenarios show improved robustness under challenging visual conditions while preserving computational efficiency and enhancing biological fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the potential of biologically grounded neural computation for robust and efficient collision perception.

title: Delay Placement Governs Feasibility and Hopf Bifurcation in a Pollution-Based Tourism Model
summary: We compare eight variants of a three-variable pollution-based tourism model obtained by assigning the same discrete delay to different terms. The delay may enter three slots: the visitor factor in the deterrence term, pollution perception, or visitation-driven growth and reinvestment. We call a placement feasible when every nonnegative initial history produces a solution that exists for all future time and remains nonnegative. For every $τ>0$, feasibility holds exactly when the visitor factor in the deterrence term is current, which occurs in four of the eight placements. In three of these four feasible placements, the positive equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable for every delay. In the fourth -- the perception-lag model, with delayed pollution perception but current visitation -- a conjugate pair of characteristic roots crosses the imaginary axis at a finite critical delay for every set of positive parameters. The equilibrium then loses stability and does not restabilise as the delay increases. A center-manifold reduction and numerical parameter sweep show that both supercritical and subcritical Hopf bifurcations can occur. The visitor-delayed placement, closest to earlier delayed-tourism models, can undergo a local Hopf bifurcation under additional conditions, but it does not preserve nonnegativity for all initial histories.

AI.tldr: Compares eight delay placements in a three-variable pollution-based tourism model, identifying which placements keep solutions nonnegative for all time and analyzing their stability and Hopf bifurcation behavior.
AI.motivation: Delay terms in tourism-pollution models can be assigned to different components, but it is unclear how the placement of the delay affects model well-posedness (existence and nonnegativity of solutions) and stability. This paper systematically compares these placements.
AI.method: The authors construct eight variants of a three-variable pollution-based tourism model by placing an identical discrete delay in different terms (deterrence visitor factor, pollution perception, or visitation-driven growth/reinvestment). They assess feasibility (global existence and nonnegativity of solutions), analyze local stability of the positive equilibrium via characteristic equations, and use center-manifold reduction plus numerical parameter sweeps to classify Hopf bifurcations.
AI.result: For every delay τ>0, feasibility holds exactly when the deterrence visitor factor is current (four of eight placements). In three of these feasible placements, the positive equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable for all delays. In the fourth (perception-lag model), a conjugate pair of characteristic roots crosses the imaginary axis at a finite critical delay for all positive parameters; the equilibrium loses stability and never restabilises. Both supercritical and subcritical Hopf bifurcations can occur. The visitor-delayed placement can undergo a local Hopf bifurcation under extra conditions but fails nonnegativity for all initial histories.
AI.conclusion: Delay placement strongly governs model feasibility and stability. Only placements keeping the deterrence visitor factor current are feasible for all delays, and instability (with Hopf bifurcations) arises specifically in the perception-lag model, while the visitor-delayed variant—closest to earlier tourism models—is not globally nonnegative.

title: Protected domains and the cost of cooperation on weighted networks
summary: A costly inherited trait can spread when its descendants create a favorable local environment. We ask which finite contact structures sustain such a collective competitor and what their advantage costs. Individuals play a donation game, conferring benefit $b$ at cost $c$. Reciprocal weighted contacts determine averaged payoffs and copying recipients, while sources are chosen globally according to payoff. Cooperation is favored when a uniformly introduced cooperator takes over more often than a defector in the complementary experiment. Exact fluctuation response and elimination of fast configurations identify the formation and competition of protected domains as the controlling processes. The sharp weak-selection threshold infima are $b/c=3$ on the four-cycle, $7$ on the five-site path, and $1$ on every fixed path with at least six sites. On the six-site path, a global bound forces near-barrier designs into this domain hierarchy. Polynomial relations among the contact ratios then control unrestricted optimization and imply eventual exact reflection symmetry. Reaching threshold $1+ε$ requires minimum contact contrast $656ε^{-2}[1+O(ε)]$ and neutral absorption time of order $ε^{-1}$. We determine their tradeoff and the associated design tolerance. Finite selection consumes the same margin. Within the controlled small-selection window, the maximal fixation advantage is of order $ε^{5/2}$ when the contrast exceeds its exact minimum by order $ε^{-1}$. Thus an improving invasion threshold can require increasing contact heterogeneity, precision and observation time.

AI.tldr: This paper studies which finite contact structures can sustain a costly cooperative trait via local environmental benefits, and analyzes the tradeoffs between invasion thresholds, contact heterogeneity, precision, and observation time.
AI.motivation: A costly inherited trait can spread if descendants create a favorable local environment, but it is unclear which finite contact structures sustain such a collective competitor and what the advantage costs.
AI.method: Individuals play a donation game giving benefit b at cost c. Reciprocal weighted contacts determine averaged payoffs and copying of recipients, while sources are chosen globally by payoff. Cooperation is favored if a uniformly introduced cooperator takes over more often than a defector in the complementary experiment. Exact fluctuation response and elimination of fast configurations identify formation and competition of protected domains.
AI.result: Sharp weak-selection threshold infima: b/c = 3 on the four-cycle, 7 on the five-site path, and 1 on every fixed path with at least six sites. On the six-site path, a global bound forces near-barrier designs into this domain hierarchy. Reaching threshold 1+ε requires minimum contact contrast 656ε^{-2}[1+O(ε)] and neutral absorption time of order ε^{-1}; their tradeoff and design tolerance are determined. Maximal fixation advantage is of order ε^{5/2} when contrast exceeds its exact minimum by order ε^{-1}.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial relations among contact ratios control unrestricted optimization and imply eventual exact reflection symmetry. An improving invasion threshold can require increasing contact heterogeneity, precision, and observation time.

title: BrainTaskonomy: Learning How to Pretrain and What to Transfer in fMRI Foundation Models
summary: fMRI foundation models increasingly aggregate heterogeneous data across brain states, cohorts, and acquisition settings, yet pretraining domains are commonly treated as a flat mixture and downstream tasks are adapted independently. We study whether measured learning relations can organize both stages without modifying the backbone. During pretraining, a lightweight Brain-DiT proxy estimates difficulty and directed facilitation across ten fMRI domains, yielding a priority-guided cumulative domain curriculum combined with high-to-low-noise timestep scheduling and joint consolidation. During adaptation, controlled first- and higher-order transfer across fifteen tasks constructs a directed taskonomy, from which budgeted integer programming (BIP) selects directly supervised source tasks and target-specific routes. The joint priority-domain and high-to-low-timestep curriculum reduces v-NMSE, PSD-NMSE, and FC-MSE by 6.5%, 16.3%, and 10.5%, respectively, relative to uniform sampling over both dimensions, and shows strong downstream performance across six in- and out-of-domain tasks. The taskonomy reveals asymmetric, target-dependent transfer, while exploratory sealed-test evaluation shows larger descriptive gains for BIP policies when higher-order route spaces are available than for matched random controls. Together, these findings support organizing fMRI pretraining and adaptation by measured learning relations rather than treating domains and tasks as independent flat sets.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes organizing fMRI foundation model pretraining and adaptation using measured learning relations instead of treating domains/tasks as flat independent sets, without modifying the backbone.
AI.motivation: fMRI foundation models aggregate heterogeneous data across brain states, cohorts, and acquisition settings, but pretraining domains are typically treated as a flat mixture and downstream tasks adapted independently, ignoring potential learning relations between them.
AI.method: A lightweight Brain-DiT proxy estimates difficulty and directed facilitation across ten fMRI domains to build a priority-guided cumulative domain curriculum with high-to-low-noise timestep scheduling and joint consolidation. For adaptation, controlled first- and higher-order transfer across fifteen tasks constructs a directed taskonomy, from which budgeted integer programming (BIP) selects source tasks and target-specific routes.
AI.result: The joint curriculum reduces v-NMSE, PSD-NMSE, and FC-MSE by 6.5%, 16.3%, and 10.5% versus uniform sampling, with strong downstream performance on six in/out-of-domain tasks. The taskonomy shows asymmetric, target-dependent transfer, and tentative sealed-test results favor BIP policies over random controls when higher-order routes are available.
AI.conclusion: Organizing fMRI pretraining and adaptation by measured learning relations, rather than treating domains and tasks as independent flat sets, improves performance without altering the backbone.
